catalog_quote: 2.4 Tone. This section describes tone levels in Gumuz and related tone rules using nouns as examples. However, the same rules apply to tonal behavior in verbs. While this section focuses mainly on tone in Northern Gumuz (NoG), the same tonal patterns and rules have been observed in Southern Gumuz (SoG). The differences in SoG tonal behavior are mentioned where applicable. 2.4.1 Tone Levels and Melodies. In Gumuz, there are two contrastive tone levels, H and L. In two syllable nouns, there are four possible tone melodies, HH, LL, HL, and LH, which are most clearly demonstrated in monomorphemic nouns. ... [pp. 15-16:] Some years later, Unseth published a brief article on the phonology of Gumuz as spoken in the village of Sirba located in Sirba Abay wereda (1989). ... In addition to his findings on lexical tone, Unseth also observed a strong correlation between stress and high tone in Gumu…

sources.citation: Uzar, Henning. 1989. Studies in Gumuz: Sese phonology and TMA system. In M. Lionel Bender (ed.), Topics in Nilo-Saharan Linguistics (Nilo-Saharan 3), 347-383. Hamburg: Helmut Buske. [Rosetta Project open excerpt, archive.org item rosettaproject_guk_phon-1: title page + pp. 347-354 only]
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or at Harvard
sources.quote: No stress statement in the open pages. p. 347: 'This chapter, therefore, concentrates on the surface structure of Gumuz phonology, mainly dealing with segments and syllables. Tone will be marked when high, low, and unmarked when mid. A more systematic tonal analysis is in progress.' Sese is identified as the informants' variety (Glottolog language_note: 'Sese = Southern Gumuz'; Ahland 2012:17 'the Sese (SoG) variety'). Confirms Gumuz/Sese is treated as tonal; the chapter's dedicated stress sections (pp. 362, 365) are outside the excerpt.
sources.note: Only first-hand phonology of a Southern Gumuz (Sese) variety with a dedicated 'Stress' section (p. 365, per the volume's detailed contents fetched sources now); our record says 'no word-stress rule is given anywhere' and rests its stress remark on Ahland's second-hand summary of Unseth. We hold only the open Rosetta excerpt pp. 347-354.

sources.citation: Bender, M. Lionel (ed.). 1989. Topics in Nilo-Saharan Linguistics (Nilo-Saharan 3). Hamburg: Buske. Front matter and Detailed Contents [Rosetta Project, archive.org item rosettaproject_guk_contents-1]
sources.quote: Table of contents only, but it shows Uzar 1989 Part 1 contains '3.2.1.1 Stress ... 362' (stress as a conditioning factor eliminated when testing vowel length), '3.2.1.3 Tone ... 362', and a stand-alone section '4. Stress ... 365' followed by '5. Syllable Patterns ... 366'. So a primary, first-hand stress section for a Southern Gumuz variety exists and is unread by us (and unreported in Ahland's literature review).
